clinicalPearls: A congenital dysplastic kidney replaced by multiple non-communicating cysts of varying size with intervening dysplastic tissue and no functioning nephrons, giving a non-functioning renal unit
Usually unilateral and detected on antenatal ultrasound; bilateral disease is incompatible with life
On ultrasound the cysts do not communicate and there is no identifiable normal renal parenchyma or a reniform pelvicalyceal pattern, distinguishing it from hydronephrosis
A DMSA or MAG3 scan confirms absent function in the affected kidney
The natural history is progressive involution, with many kidneys shrinking or disappearing over months to years

The contralateral kidney should be assessed carefully, as compensatory hypertrophy is expected and coexisting anomalies such as reflux or ureteropelvic junction obstruction on the other side carry the main functional prognosis

Most cases are managed conservatively with surveillance; nephrectomy is reserved for the rare complications of a very large lesion, symptoms, hypertension, or diagnostic uncertainty (concern for malignancy)
reference.pathophysiology: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a severe form of renal dysplasia thought to result from an early developmental insult, such as complete ureteric or ureteropelvic obstruction/atresia, that disrupts the normal inductive interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric blastema. The affected kidney develops as a disorganised collection of non-communicating cysts with dysplastic stroma and cartilage and no functioning nephron mass. Because the collecting system does not connect, the unit produces no urine and typically involutes over time. Unlike hydronephrosis, there is no central dilated pelvis draining the cysts.
additionalDifferentials: Severe hydronephrosis from ureteropelvic junction obstruction
Autosomal recessive or dominant polycystic kidney disease
Cystic renal tumour (e.g. cystic nephroma, cystic Wilms)
Segmental multicystic dysplasia in a duplex system
Obstructed dysplastic kidney with retained function
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound to demonstrate non-communicating cysts and absent normal parenchyma
DMSA or MAG3 scintigraphy to confirm the kidney is non-functioning
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) if contralateral or ipsilateral reflux is suspected
Serial ultrasound to monitor involution and the contralateral kidney
MRI in cases of diagnostic uncertainty
redFlags: Any abnormality of the contralateral solitary functioning kidney
New-onset hypertension attributable to the dysplastic kidney
Enlarging or solid components within the lesion raising concern for malignancy
Respiratory or renal compromise suggesting bilateral disease in the neonate
reference.prognosis: For unilateral disease with a normal contralateral kidney the outlook is generally excellent, with progressive involution and good overall renal function; prognosis depends chiefly on the health of the contralateral kidney, and rare complications such as hypertension are the main reasons for intervention.
pitfalls: Confusing multicystic dysplastic kidney with severe hydronephrosis and mismanaging accordingly
Neglecting thorough evaluation and follow-up of the contralateral kidney
Performing unnecessary nephrectomy on a lesion that would involute
Overlooking rare malignant transformation or a coexisting tumour
management: Conservative management with serial renal ultrasound to follow the expected involution of the affected kidney
Regular blood pressure monitoring with antihypertensive treatment if hypertension develops
Careful assessment and protection of the contralateral kidney, managing any coexisting vesicoureteric reflux or pelviureteric junction obstruction
Nephrectomy reserved for complications such as uncontrolled hypertension, mass effect or diagnostic uncertainty regarding malignancy
Micturating cystourethrogram where reflux is suspected
Longitudinal monitoring of renal function, since prognosis depends chiefly on the healthy contralateral kidney
Referral to paediatric nephrology and urology for surveillance
